fields.Front: Why are rocks the most stable and oldest records of past events?
fields.Back: The chemical bonds in the most common rock type, silicates, are extremely hard to break.

fields.Front: What ages for Earth's origin did the Maya and Hindu calendars suggest?
fields.Back: Maya: more than 400 million years; Hindu: almost 2 billion years (versus Ussher's 6000 years).

fields.Text: The oldest matter, meteorites from {{c1::primitive asteroids}}, is consistently {{c2::4.567}} billion years old - the rough age of the {{c3::Solar System}}.
fields.Extra: Meteorites from primitive asteroids, representing material formed as the Solar System took shape: consistently 4.567 billion years (rough age of the Solar System).

fields.Text: Earth's age, {{c1::4.54 billion years}}, is taken from the average age of {{c2::meteorites (asteroid fragments)}}, the same solids from which Earth accreted.
fields.Extra: 4.54 billion years - the average age of meteorites (asteroid fragments), because Earth accreted from the same solids.

fields.Text: Age of the Solar System: {{c1::4.567}} Ga. Age of Earth: {{c2::4.54}} Ga. Oldest mineral (zircon): {{c3::4.404}} Ga.
The oldest mineral on Earth is a crystal of {{c1::zircon}}, dated at {{c2::4.404}} billion years.
fields.Extra: A zircon crystal, 4.404 billion years old.

fields.Text: About {{c1::4.48}} billion years ago a {{c2::Mars}}-sized planet called {{c3::Theia}} hit Earth, completely melting both bodies.
fields.Extra: A Mars-sized planet that impacted Earth about 4.48 billion years ago, completely melting both bodies (its debris formed the Moon).

fields.Front: Why can't we find a chunk of the very oldest Earth rock?
fields.Back: Plate tectonics constantly recycles old material.

fields.Front: Notation: what do Ga, Ma, ka and a stand for?
fields.Back: Ga = billion years; Ma = million years; ka = thousand years; a = year. 4.567 Ga = 4,567 Ma = 4,567,000,000 a.

fields.Front: Name the two oldest crustal fragments on Earth (both in Canada) and their ages.
fields.Back: Acasta Gneiss, NWT: 4.031 +/- 0.003 Ga; Nuvvuagittuq Greenstone, Quebec: 4.388 Ga or 3.75 Ga (disputed).

fields.Front: What is relative age dating?
fields.Back: Determining the order of geological events (older vs younger) without numerical ages, using the principles of stratigraphy.

fields.Front: What three logical arguments underlie Steno's principles?
fields.Back: Sedimentary layers are deposited on top of each other as particles settle from water; the layers are flat when deposited (large water body); they are deposited over wide areas (oceans).

fields.Front: State the Principle of Superposition.
fields.Back: In an undeformed vertical sequence of sedimentary strata, the oldest layers are at the base and the youngest at the top; it also applies to the fossils the layers contain.

fields.Front: State the Principle of Original Horizontality.
fields.Back: Sedimentary strata lay flat (horizontal) when first deposited, so steeply inclined rocks have experienced a later deforming process.

fields.Front: State the Principle of Original Lateral Continuity.
fields.Back: Flat-lying strata initially extended in all directions; similar strata on either side of a valley or ocean were originally continuous.

fields.Text: Steno's three principles ('Steno's Laws'): {{c1::Superposition}}, {{c2::Original Horizontality}}, {{c3::Original Lateral Continuity}}.

fields.Front: What does the word 'strata' mean and where does it come from?
fields.Back: Sedimentary rock layers; from the Latin word for 'bed'.

fields.Front: What is an unconformity?
fields.Back: A horizon representing a time break during which erosion of a rock sequence took place before deposition of a more recent sequence; studied by Hutton in the 1780s-90s.

fields.Front: Define angular unconformity.
fields.Back: An unconformity where the beds above and below have different slopes (e.g. tilted beds A-E under flat bed G).

fields.Front: Define disconformity.
fields.Back: An unconformity where the beds above and below are parallel but there is a time gap (e.g. between J and K).

fields.Front: Define non-conformity.
fields.Back: An unconformity where sedimentary layers rest on or are intruded by igneous rocks (e.g. between igneous F and sedimentary G).

fields.Text: Three kinds of unconformity: {{c1::angular unconformity}} (different dips), {{c2::disconformity}} (parallel beds, time gap), {{c3::non-conformity}} (igneous rock below sediments).

fields.Front: State the three rules of the Principle of Cross-Cutting Relationships.
fields.Back: A fault is younger than the youngest rock it cuts; strata above an unconformity are younger than those below; any feature that cuts across a rock is younger than the rock it cuts.

fields.Front: Whose principle is Cross-Cutting Relationships, and what gap in Steno's Laws did it fill?
fields.Back: James Hutton's; it explains igneous intrusions and the relationship between an eroded rock and the strata laid on top of it.

fields.Text: {{c1::William 'Strata' Smith}}, a {{c2::canal engineer}} in southern England, matched layers by their fossils, founding the Principle of {{c3::Faunal Succession}}.
fields.Extra: A canal engineer in southern England who noticed each layer contained characteristic fossils and was first to identify the same layer in different places by fossil content - the Principle of Faunal Succession.

fields.Front: State the Principle of Faunal Succession.
fields.Back: Sedimentary layers contain characteristic fossils distinct from those above and below, so layers in different places can be correlated (matched in age) by their fossil content, using reference horizons.

fields.Front: List the five principles of stratigraphy and their authors.
fields.Back: Superposition, Original Horizontality, Original Lateral Continuity (Steno); Cross-Cutting Relationships (Hutton); Faunal Succession (Smith).

fields.Text: The five principles of stratigraphy: Steno's three, Hutton's {{c1::Cross-Cutting Relationships}}, and Smith's {{c2::Faunal Succession}}.

fields.Front: What is a composite stratigraphic column and how was it built?
fields.Back: A younger-upon-older vertical sequence assembled by correlating strata from region to region (superposition, cross-cutting, faunal succession) until a world-wide column was compiled.

fields.Front: How were subdivisions of geologic time designated?
fields.Back: Subdivisions of the stratigraphic column became time divisions; boundaries were placed where fossil types change - the emergence and extinction of fossil life forms.

fields.Text: An {{c1::era}} is a long interval of geologic time separated from the next by a {{c2::major extinction event}}.
fields.Extra: A long interval of geologic time separated from the next by a major extinction event.

fields.Front: What two events did early palaeontologists use to make the major era boundaries?
fields.Back: Two global extinction events: between the Palaeozoic and Mesozoic eras (251 Ma) and between the Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras (65.5 Ma).

fields.Text: Era names: Palaeozoic = '{{c1::ancient life}}', Mesozoic = '{{c2::middle life}}', Cenozoic = '{{c3::recent life}}'.
The Palaeozoic/Mesozoic boundary is dated at {{c1::251}} million years ago; the Mesozoic/Cenozoic boundary at {{c2::65.5}} million years ago.
'Precambrian' is {{c1::not}} a formal time division; it lumps all time before the {{c2::Palaeozoic}} Era, and life {{c3::did}} develop during it.
fields.Extra: No. It simply lumps all time before the Palaeozoic Era. It originally meant 'time before life', but life actually developed in the Precambrian.

fields.Front: Geologic time scale: list the Palaeozoic periods from oldest to youngest.
fields.Back: Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian.

fields.Front: Geologic time scale: list the Mesozoic periods from oldest to youngest.
fields.Back: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous.

fields.Front: Geologic time scale: name the Cenozoic periods and the epochs of the Quaternary.
fields.Back: Tertiary (Paleocene, Eocene, Oligocene, Miocene, Pliocene) and Quaternary (Pleistocene, Holocene).

fields.Front: Geologic time scale: which period begins with the 'explosion of organisms with shells' and when?
fields.Back: The Cambrian, about 545 million years ago (base of the Palaeozoic).

fields.Front: Geologic time scale (Fig. 7): approximate base ages of the Cambrian, Permian, Triassic and Cretaceous.
fields.Back: Cambrian 545 Ma; Permian 290 Ma; Triassic 245 Ma (text: 251); Cretaceous 146 Ma.

fields.Front: Geologic time scale: in which period did dinosaurs and mammals first appear, and in which did birds and flowering plants appear?
fields.Back: Dinosaurs and mammals: Triassic. Birds: Jurassic. Flowering plants: Cretaceous.

fields.Front: Geologic time scale: when did free oxygen in the atmosphere / an ozone layer appear, and the first fossils?
fields.Back: Free oxygen and ozone about 2500 Ma; primitive life (first fossils) about 3500 Ma - both Precambrian.

fields.Text: Order of eras from oldest to youngest: Precambrian (informal), {{c1::Palaeozoic}}, {{c2::Mesozoic}}, {{c3::Cenozoic}}.
{{c1::Henri Becquerel}} discovered radioactivity in {{c2::1896}}: some atoms (e.g. uranium) are unstable and break down predictably.
fields.Extra: Henri Becquerel, 1896: some atoms of some elements (e.g. uranium) are unstable and break down predictably.

fields.Text: Atomic number = number of {{c1::protons}} (same for every atom of an element); atomic mass = protons plus {{c2::neutrons}}.
fields.Extra: Atomic number = number of protons (same for all atoms of an element). Atomic mass = protons + neutrons. (The reading labels them A and Z respectively.)

fields.Text: {{c1::Isotopes}} are atoms of the same element that differ in the number of {{c2::neutrons}} in the nucleus, and thus in {{c3::mass}}.
fields.Extra: Atoms of the same element that differ in the number of neutrons in the nucleus, and thus in mass. They behave the same chemically (heavier ones react slightly slower).

fields.Text: Hydrogen has three isotopes (masses 1, 2, 3); the mass-{{c1::3}} isotope (1 proton + {{c2::2}} neutrons) is the {{c3::radioactive}} one.
fields.Extra: Mass 1: 1 proton, 0 neutrons (stable); mass 2: 1 proton, 1 neutron (stable); mass 3: 1 proton, 2 neutrons (radioactive).

fields.Front: Define radioactivity.
fields.Back: The progressive breakdown (decay) of the nucleus of an atom or isotope; each radioactive isotope decays at its own characteristic rate, which has never changed.

fields.Front: What are 'parent' and 'daughter' isotopes?
fields.Back: Parent = the original isotope in a decay step; daughter = the isotope (of a different element) produced by that step.

fields.Text: The {{c1::half-life}} is the period of time in which exactly {{c2::half}} the nuclei of a radioactive species decay.
fields.Extra: The period of time in which exactly half the nuclei of a radioactive species decay (in any step of the breakdown).

fields.Front: Why is radioactive decay called exponential?
fields.Back: Each half-life, exactly half of the remaining parents decay, so the number of daughters produced is large at first and becomes smaller and smaller as fewer parents remain.

fields.Text: After 1 half-life the parent:daughter ratio is {{c1::50:50}}; after 2 half-lives {{c2::25:75}}; after about {{c3::10}} half-lives the parent is too small to measure.

fields.Front: Half-life of uranium-235 and its daughter?
fields.Back: U-235 -> Pb-207 (lead-207); 704 million years.

fields.Front: Half-life of rubidium-87 and its daughter?
fields.Back: Rb-87 -> Sr-87 (strontium-87); 48.8 billion years.

fields.Front: Half-life of potassium-40 and its daughter?
fields.Back: K-40 -> Ar-40 (argon-40); 1.26 billion years.

fields.Front: Half-life of carbon-14, its daughter, and its useful range?
fields.Back: C-14 -> N-14 (nitrogen-14, per slides); 5730 years; used for organic material younger than about 50,000 years (all gone after 10 half-lives, ~57,000 years).

fields.Text: Half-lives: U-235 = {{c1::704 million}} years; K-40 = {{c2::1.26 billion}} years; Rb-87 = {{c3::48.8 billion}} years.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of {{c1::5730}} years and is useful for organic samples younger than about {{c2::50,000}} years.

fields.Front: If three isotope systems are analysed in one granite, what result is expected, and why is only one used in practice?
fields.Back: All three should give the same age; only one is used because analytical costs are high.

fields.Text: {{c1::Zircon}} is the mineral used for {{c2::uranium-lead}} dating of igneous rocks because it contains uranium.
fields.Extra: Zircon, because it contains uranium; the U:Pb ratio in the crystal gives its age.

fields.Front: What is a 'closed system' in radiometric dating?
fields.Back: A rock/mineral that has neither gained nor lost parent or daughter atoms since it formed, so the ratio reflects only elapsed time.

fields.Front: Why does carbon-14 dating work on once-living things?
fields.Back: All living things take in carbon (including C-14); after death intake stops and the C-14 decays, so the remaining fraction gives time since death.

fields.Front: CALC: A rock has a K-40:Ar-40 ratio of 25:75. Age?
fields.Back: 25% parent = 2 half-lives; 2 x 1.26 Ga = 2.52 billion years.

fields.Front: CALC: A zircon retains 12.5% of its U-235. Age?
fields.Back: 12.5% = 1/8 = 3 half-lives; 3 x 704 Ma = 2,112 million years (~2.1 Ga).

fields.Front: CALC: Charcoal has 1/4 of the C-14 of living wood. Age?
fields.Back: 1/4 = 2 half-lives; 2 x 5730 = 11,460 years.

fields.Front: Why can't carbon-14 date a dinosaur bone or a 2-billion-year-old granite?
fields.Back: After ~10 half-lives (~57,000 years) no measurable C-14 remains; 65.5 Ma or 2 Ga is thousands to millions of half-lives.

fields.Front: Why can sediments usually not be dated absolutely (slides)?
fields.Back: Their grains are recycled from older rocks, so an isotopic age would date the source rock, not the deposition; relative dating is used instead.
